item.title: NWSL final sees pro-trans protesters have spats with women's sports advocates but no violence or ejections
item.description: Jennifer Sey says her group faced boos but no ejections at the NWSL championship at Audi Field, as trans pride flags flew during Kansas City's 2-1 win.
item.content:encoded:
Women's sports advocate Jennifer Sey attended Saturday's National Women's Soccer League championship without interference from security, despite encountering hostile spectators and seeing prominent transgender-rights displays throughout the stadium.

Sey, the founder of XX-XY Athletics, attended the championship at Audi Field alongside former NWSL player Elizabeth Eddy and other supporters of protecting female-only sports.

The group had announced its plans to attend days earlier, raising questions about whether stadium officials would allow them to remain if other fans objected to their apparel after fellow "Save Women's Sports" advocates were struck by pro-trans activists at a Portland Thorns game before being ejected, last month. In September, fans wearing XX-XY Athletics shirts were also ejected from a Thorns game.

NWSL BOSS SAYS ALL FANS ARE 'WELCOME' AHEAD OF FINAL AFTER MULTIPLE EJECTIONS OF WOMEN'S SPORTS ADVOCATES

But Sey said the reception on Saturday in Washington, D.C., was considerably calmer than she anticipated.

"I didn't expect that, honestly. I expected the energy to be a little more aggressive in our direction," Sey told OutKick. "But generally speaking, it was fine. No one bothered us, so good for them. That's what you should do."

Sey said the group initially encountered hostility at the league's Fan Fest at The Wharf, where some attendees shouted insults as they walked past.

"People were definitely rude, definitely kind of would walk by and say, 'Boo, you're a transphobe,' and yell at us," she said.

Inside Audi Field, Sey said one woman gave her a thumbs-down gesture and booed. She also said Eddy, who was seated several rows ahead of her, reported that another spectator repeatedly shouted at Eddy and her companion as they moved through the seating area.

According to Sey, Eddy was told, "You don't belong here. You should leave."

FANS DISAGREE WITH PORTLAND THORNS OVER REASON FOR EJECTION IN XX-XY APPAREL DISPUTE: 'THEY ARE LYING'

But the confrontations never escalated into the physical altercations or security interventions that characterized previous incidents involving XX-XY Athletics supporters.

"No one gave us any problems," Sey said when asked specifically about stadium personnel. "Just little dumb things here and there. People, you know, giving us the finger, saying, 'Boo,' someone told others, 'You don't belong here.' But I don't care about that stuff."

While Sey and her guests were able to watch the match without major disruption, transgender-rights messaging was prominently displayed among spectators, particularly in the supporters' section behind one of the goals.

Images and video from Saturday's championship show a large transgender pride flag on an extended pole, along with banners bearing the messages "Protect Trans Lives" and "Trans People Belong in Sports."

The displays were visible near a section of supporters dressed in matching gear, although Sey emphasized that most spectators throughout the stadium appeared to be wearing ordinary team apparel.

She estimated seeing approximately 20 to 30 people visibly participating in the transgender-rights displays, while acknowledging that she could not account for every spectator.

"It wasn't ... like Portland," Sey said, contrasting the atmosphere with previous confrontations at Portland Thorns games. "It was more just there were a few big ones."

She also questioned the presence of the large flags at the championship.

"Why do you think it's correct to bring a trans flag to a soccer game?" Sey asked. "I mean, that's activism, not fandom."

However, Sey said she did not know whether the displays had anything to do with her group's attendance and suspected the flags would have been present regardless.

"I don't think they had those because of us," she said. "Maybe. I mean, I have no way of knowing."

The size of at least one flagpole also caught Sey's attention, particularly following an October incident in Portland in which women's sports advocates reported being struck with flagpoles.

"Are they really allowed to bring that in?" Sey asked. "That seems like a weapon to me."

Audi Field's published stadium guidelines permit large signs, flags and banners in designated supporters' sections, subject to restrictions. Flagpoles generally must be constructed from hollow, half-inch PVC pipe and may not exceed 3.5 feet without advance approval from stadium management. The guidelines also require flags and banners to be approved.

THE CRAIG CARTON SHOW–UNFILTERED, UNAPOLOGETIC AND UNMISSABLE. DOWNLOAD HIS DAILY PODCAST NOW!

Saturday's relatively peaceful outcome followed public assurances from NWSL Commissioner Jessica Berman, who addressed concerns about fan treatment during her State of the League press conference Thursday.

The commissioner was questioned about previous ejections of women's sports advocates and potential conflicts between those spectators and established NWSL supporters' groups.

"We expect the people who come into our buildings, no matter their points of view, to be there to enjoy the excitement and the incredible athleticism of our players and the competition on the field," Berman said. "And if people are there for that reason, they are 100% welcome."

Berman also emphasized the importance of established supporters' groups, calling them the "lifeblood of this league."

She explained that the NWSL takes a hybrid approach to stadium rules, maintaining minimum leaguewide standards while giving individual clubs discretion over certain decisions.

"And it's our job to make sure that we enforce those policies consistently across all of our stadiums," Berman said.

On Sept. 6, eight spectators were removed from Providence Park after displaying apparel with messages supporting female-only sports. The Thorns maintained that the group violated stadium rules by distributing unapproved materials, an explanation the attendees disputed.

A more volatile confrontation occurred Oct. 23, when approximately 20 supporters wearing XX-XY Athletics shirts displayed a large "Save Women's Sports" banner during a Thorns match against the North Carolina Courage.

CLICK HERE FOR MORE OUTKICK SPORTS COVERAGE

Video captured spectators confronting the group, including incidents involving flagpoles, before security forcibly removed several participants.

The Department of Justice subsequently confirmed it was reviewing the incident for potential civil rights concerns. The circumstances surrounding the removals have remained disputed.

The NWSL's published fan code of conduct prohibits threatening, abusive or discriminatory behavior, as well as provoking such conduct. It also restricts certain forms of political campaigning and advocacy concerning candidates, parties and legislation.

Ahead of Saturday's championship, Sey had said she would not voluntarily abandon plans to attend if her apparel attracted complaints.

"I bought these tickets weeks ago. I'm not changing my plans," Sey previously told OutKick. "We have every right to be there."

She also said she wanted to attend primarily to enjoy professional women's soccer, particularly watching Washington Spirit star Trinity Rodman.

On the field, the Kansas City Current defeated the Washington Spirit 2-1 to claim the franchise's first NWSL championship. Vanessa DiBernardo and Debinha scored for Kansas City, while Rodman scored Washington's lone goal in stoppage time.

The defeat marked the Spirit's third consecutive loss in the NWSL championship game.

item.title: Stephen A Smith isn't the only one who knows dissing White people comes without consequences
item.description: Stephen A. Smith doubled down on his Lakers take even after Jay Williams and Kwame Brown pushed back, fueling a debate over race in sports commentary.
item.content:encoded:
Want to sound edgy without actually taking a risk? Want to go viral knowing you won't face a single meaningful consequence? Here's a foolproof strategy.

Disparage someone for being White.

I've heard a few times that we're past peak wokeness — when the slightest rhetorical misstep could land you on the unemployment line. Perhaps the success of events such as the "Roast of Tom Brady" — where comedians gave a massive middle finger to political correctness — suggests that is true.

But one thing still seems as fashionable as ever: Clowning on a Caucasian.

STEPHEN A. SMITH SAYS WHITE PLAYERS ARE NOT GOOD ENOUGH TO WIN NBA CHAMPIONSHIPS

ESPN's Stephen A. Smith was the latest high-profile sports personality to lean into that trend when he suggested the Lakers' three best players are too White to contend for a championship.

"I do not think that they’re getting past the second round," he said. "Not a team with its top three players being White dudes."

He hasn't budged from that position despite former NBA players such as Jay Williams and Kwame Brown — both of whom are Black — calling him out. Smith has even said that the color of the Lakers' Big Three (referred to by some as "Snowtime") should be a motivating factor for the "brothers" in the league.

Do I think Stephen A. should be disciplined for his comments? No. The threshold for speech punishment should be higher than that. But is there any chance in the world a White guy talking that way about, say, three Black NHL players would keep his job? I think we know the answer.

But Smith's remarks about the Lakers are hardly an isolated example of how casually White people can be dismissed because of their race. Last month, former NBA player Charlie Villanueva suggested that Mavericks star Cooper Flagg couldn't be the face of today's NBA because he was White.

WILL CAIN CHALLENGES STEPHEN A SMITH ON 'RACIST' CLAIM ABOUT 'WHITE DUDES' IN THE NBA

"It's a Black league, right?" Villanueva said. "Am I lying? Majority rules."

I'm not sure if Villanueva watches a lot of golf, but for about 25 years, everybody was rooting for the Black guy. Moreover, if an analyst suggested that Tiger Woods couldn't be the face of golf because it's a majority-White sport, no apology would be able to rescue his career.

Want to take this beyond sports? In June of this year, former ESPN host Jemele Hill responded to a Threads question asking what people would do if they woke up White, saying, "I'm going to apply for a job with a great salary knowing I have no qualifications and will get the job."

Want to take this beyond sports personalities? Last year, then-Democratic Rep. Jasmine Crockett went on CNN and complained about "white tears" from "mediocre white boys" who, she suggested, couldn't compete with more qualified minorities.

Nobody should be discouraged from talking about race, which can be one of the more terrifying topics to address. But there's a difference between discussing racial issues and casually stereotyping people because of their skin color. The ease with which White people can be dismissed or generalized is striking.

JASMINE CROCKETT BLASTS HER TEXAS DEMOCRATIC PRIMARY LOSS AS ‘RACIST RACE'

Any other race, though?

Just look at what people have been apologizing for lately. In July, Toronto Tempo coach Sandy Brondello complained to referees that Angel Reese was a "protected species" after a controversial foul call.

Brondello, who is Australian, was using a familiar Australian sports expression for an athlete who receives favorable treatment from officials. But the comment was interpreted by some as racially offensive. So she gave a public mea culpa, specifically acknowledging its impact on Black women, and the WNBA suspended her for one game without pay.

And then there was Braiden Bell, who was fired as the Blazers' play-by-play announcer in October less than 12 hours after getting the job. The reason? A local TV station dug up tweets from 2012 — when Bell was 15 years old — including one in which he said, "I'm not racist at all...But not gonna lie...Asian people piss me off!"

Yes, that was an incredibly stupid thing for Bell to put out into the world when he was an adolescent. But compare that to Sarah Jeong, who was hired by The New York Times editorial board in 2018 despite a history of tweets disparaging White people — including one in which she admitted getting a "sick" amount of joy from being cruel to old White men.

The Times acknowledged that her comments were inappropriate but stood by its decision to hire her.

So one broadcaster loses his dream job over something he tweeted at 15, while another journalist lands one of the most prestigious jobs in the business despite similarly ugly remarks about a different race.

Absurd? Yes. Surprising? No.

I don't want to sound like a prude here who thinks that White people should be off-limits. There's nothing wrong with acknowledging trends, and there's nothing wrong with making jokes.

CLICK HERE FOR MORE OUTKICK SPORTS COVERAGE

One of my favorite Dave Chappelle sketches involved him recruiting John Mayer to play electric guitar in front of unsuspecting White people, who immediately started dancing as though they were under some kind of spell. It was hilarious. And if you can't laugh at that, you might need to lighten up.

But I also remember watching an episode of "Ted Lasso" about three years back, in which one character asks another whether playing miniature golf is better than watching polo with "a bunch of old white men."

"Definitely," comes the response. The first character then adds that the dinosaurs at the miniature golf course are probably less handsy.

THE CRAIG CARTON SHOW–UNFILTERED, UNAPOLOGETIC AND UNMISSABLE. DOWNLOAD HIS DAILY PODCAST NOW!

Fair enough. Still, notice how "old White men" was tossed in there as though that were an insult in itself. The joke was about creepy men. Their race was apparently just an added bonus.

The word "racist" gets thrown around way too casually these days. I'm not going to accuse someone like Stephen A. Smith of being that. But you don't have to be a racist to say something stupid about race. And you don't have to be offended by a joke to recognize a double standard.

Perhaps the most remarkable thing about disparaging White people is how unremarkable it's become. We hear it from sports commentators, politicians, comedians and journalists, and barely give it a second thought.

Change the skin color, though, and suddenly everyone remembers what prejudice looks like.

What do you think about this double standard? Let me know at matthew.calkins@outkick.com

item.title: College football’s quiet Saturday turns into a Big Ten disaster with brutal CFP consequences
item.description: Michigan's three-overtime upset of No. 4 UCLA, plus a QB injury, leaves the Big Ten's College Football Playoff picture in chaos with one week left.
item.content:encoded:
It was supposed to be a relatively quiet Saturday. But we should know by now that the 2026 college football season doesn’t do quiet, as the Big Ten found out.

An afternoon of teams handling business before rivalry weekend arrived over the next six days would have been the easy route. But, we should have known that there would be some type of madness that shook up the College Football Playoff race.

I just don’t think most of us woke up expecting the Big Ten to spend the day stepping on its own playoff ambitions.

For the first time since 2009, excluding the COVID season, Saturday’s schedule featured zero matchups between AP Top 25 teams. Apparently, nobody told the sport that it was supposed to take a breath.

Now, after losses by No. 4 UCLA and No. 8 Indiana, the Big Ten heads into the final week of the regular season with some uncomfortable questions.

INDIANA'S NATIONAL CHAMPIONSHIP DEFENSE ON THE BRINK AFTER OVERTIME UPSET TO WASHINGTON

If one game carried an obvious upset warning, it was UCLA’s trip to Michigan. The Wolverines have spent most of this season showing flashes of talent without consistently putting the pieces together.

On Saturday, they finally did enough to send shockwaves through the playoff race, while leaving the Bruins in shambles.

A three-overtime win over No. 4 UCLA was disruptive on its own, but the Bruins have another major problem to deal with.

On a run in the fourth quarter, quarterback Ty Dieffenbach went down with what looked like a hip injury that led to him being carted off the field.

THE CRAIG CARTON SHOW–UNFILTERED, UNAPOLOGETIC AND UNMISSABLE. DOWNLOAD HIS DAILY PODCAST NOW!

So, not only did the Bruins lose their first game of the season, they might’ve also lost their second quarterback of the season with no wiggle-room for another loss.

What does this mean? Well, UCLA do not have the strength of schedule to help their case, with a showdown against USC looming next week. The CFP committee has made it clear that they weigh the health of key players, and it gets no bigger than the starting quarterback.

Can third-string quarterback Madden Iamaleava, the brother of former starter Nico Iamaleava, lead UCLA past its biggest rival?

The answer could determine both the Bruins’ playoff position and whether they reach the Big Ten championship game.

On the other side of the country, it was No. 8 Indiana that has left the Big Ten conference in a rough spot.

After switching quarterbacks in the second half, Curt Cignetti turned to Josh Hoover in hopes of getting the Hoosiers out of Seattle with a win.

Unfortunately for Indiana, its CFP hopes took a massive hit with the overtime loss after kicker Paddy McAteer missed the 37-yard field goal that would have sent the game into double-OT.

If there was a top-10 team that couldn’t afford this kind of loss, it was Indiana.

Now, Indiana must beat Purdue and hope the results elsewhere create a path to the Big Ten championship game. A UCLA loss to USC offers one possible opening. An Oregon loss could bring additional tiebreaker scenarios into play.

Either way, the Hoosiers need help.

FIFTH-RANKED TEXAS DOMINATES ARKANSAS AS ARCH MANNING IS HEATING UP AHEAD OF THE COLLEGE FOOTBALL PLAYOFF

Simply put, Indiana now finds itself on the outside looking in. A spot in the playoff is essentially out the window unless they win the Big Ten Championship.

Lane Kiffin left Neyland Stadium through an alternative exit Saturday night. The Vols left with a clear path toward the postseason with the 27-13 win.

Tennessee's defense has carried this team all season, in addition to running back DeSean Bishop, with LSU getting a front row seat to the show on Saturday night inside Neyland Stadium. The Vols had a reservation in the Tigers backfield, finishing the game with eight sacks and forcing three turnovers.

LANE KIFFIN TAKES THE SIDE EXIT AS TENNESSEE SENDS LSU HOME AND MOVES TO THE DOORSTEP OF CFP

The most consequential home game in recent memory for Tennessee turned Neyland Stadium into a hornets nest that even Lane Kiffin admitted was a major factor in the Vols win.

Now comes one final regular-season stop: Vanderbilt.

A win in Nashville would put Tennessee into the playoff and potentially hosting a game in December. But before the Vols could entertain any of that, they had to handle an LSU team that is now limping toward the finish with five losses.

They did exactly that.

Along the Bayou, the questions are getting louder. How does a roster carrying a more than $40 million price tag produce this kind of season?

The problems keep piling up for Kiffin, and the offseason probably can’t arrive soon enough for LSU fans.

In other news around the SEC, it was No. 14 Kentucky that saw its CFP hopes officially end on the road at Missouri, while No. 1 Georgia took care of No. 21 South Carolina after a first half scare.

Next up, it's rivalry weekend with plenty of eyes on what happens between No. 3 Alabama against Auburn and No. 5 Texas playing Texas A&M in College Station.

Right now, it looks as though the conference could end up earning four CFP bids.

Of course, that assumes Thanksgiving weekend doesn’t deliver another round of madness.

It's officially over for No. 14 Ohio State, after losing on the road at Nebraska. The Cornhuskers snapped a 31-game losing streak against AP top-25 opponents in the win over the Buckeyes. But, Jeremiah Smith might have earned the Heisman Trophy in the loss, with 165 yards and 2 touchdowns.

As for the Big 12, Texas Tech moved one step closer to playing for a CFP spot. If the No. 12 Red Raiders beat TCU on Thanksgiving night, they will play Utah for a conference championship.

Can No. 10 BYU also sneak into the College Football Playoff? Well, if Texas Tech loses to TCU, the Cougars could play for a Big 12 title, setting up a rematch with Utah.

But, would the CFP committee potentially give the conference three bids into the postseason?

CLICK HERE FOR MORE OUTKICK SPORTS COVERAGE

I guess we'll find out soon enough.

In the ACC, it was No. 7 Miami surviving against Virginia Tech in the 28-20 win. There was a point in this game where the Hokies actually led 14-0, before the Hurricanes put together the comeback behind running back Mark Fletcher, while Darian Mensah finished the game with two interceptions.

After destroying Georgia Tech, it will be Wake Forest playing Miami for an ACC championship in two weeks. If both teams win next week, they should both receive a CFP spot.

Oh, and is there a Group of Six team that would like to participate in the College Football Playoff?

After San Diego State shocked No. 17 Boise State on a last-second field goal, we've reached the point of just throwing our hands in the air.

At this point, does anybody want to make the committee’s job easier? I didn’t think so.

Tuesday’s rankings will offer our next look at how the committee views this mess. If the past two weeks are any indication, the explanations might leave us with even more questions.

Buckle up. Rivalry week has plenty to work with.

item.title: Indonesia candy factory fire leaves multiple dead, dozens missing
item.description: A massive fire tore through PT Fonusa Agung Mulia's candy factory in Indonesia's Banten, killing at least three with up to 50 workers missing.
item.content:encoded:
A massive fire tore through a three-story candy factory in Indonesia's Banten province, killing at least three workers and likely more, and leaving dozens of others unaccounted for as emergency crews fought persistent hotspots into Sunday.

Indonesian police removed 24 body bags amid battling the smoldering fire and pausing a search for missing workers overnight, which will resume Monday morning. There were reportedly as many as 300 present for their Saturday shift, but the factory said 24 of the 65 workers involved had returned home, four were receiving medical treatment, 29 remained missing and the whereabouts of another eight had yet to be confirmed.

Body bags might contain remains from several people because the intensity of the fire had rendered the recovered victims unidentifiable, police said.

The fire broke out at 5 p.m. local time Saturday at the PT Fonusa Agung Mulia facility in the Cikande area of the Serang district, which borders the capital, Jakarta.

CHINA FIREWORKS FACTORY EXPLOSION: VIDEO CAPTURES DEVASTATING AFTERMATH OF BLAST THAT LEFT AT LEAST 26 DEAD

"We have concluded that the victims of this fire cannot be identified through visual inspection," Wahyu Hidayati, a police disaster victim identification official, said.

Authorities are collecting DNA samples from relatives and personal belongings of the missing workers. The identification process could take two to three weeks, Hidayati added.

WASHINGTON PAPER MILL CHEMICAL TANK IMPLODES, KILLING AT LEAST 1 AND LEAVING 9 MISSING

Flames engulfed the structure and sent thick black smoke billowing into the sky, leaving behind twisted metal and blackened, corrugated iron roofing.

FIRE ABOARD CARGO SHIP UNDERGOING REPAIRS AT BUSY CHINESE PORT LEAVES 25 PEOPLE DEAD, FIVE MORE INJURED

"The figure of 50 refers to those whom we have not yet been able to account for, " the factory owner said during a news conference.

More than 12 hours after the fire started, 15 fire trucks backed by water cannons were still working to douse hotspots concentrated in the central and rear sections of the building. A joint response team comprising police, military personnel, the Indonesian Red Cross, and volunteers was there, though structural instability made their work difficult.

SEATTLE FIRE CREWS RESPOND TO 3-ALARM INDUSTRIAL DISTRICT WAREHOUSE FIRE, ROOF PARTIALLY COLLAPSES

"We are conducting sweeps in the areas that have already been brought under control, " Tubagus Mahfud, operations chief of the Serang fire department, said. "Parts of the structure had collapsed, while poor lighting conditions required firefighters to proceed cautiously."

Mahfud warned that the factory's production materials posed a high risk of reignition, making thorough cooling operations critical before crews can access the entire building.

MASSIVE CHEMICAL FIRE ERUPTS AT ELECTRICAL TRANSFORMER PLANT IN MISSISSIPPI, FORCING EVACUATION

"Authorities continue to coordinate with families and the company to determine the whereabouts of employees believed to have been inside the factory when the fire broke out," the Banten Search and Rescue Agency's Rizky Dwianto said.

While police said the cause of the fire remains under investigation, survivors told Indonesian media the flames originated from a cooling unit on the third floor.

The facility is part of Indonesia's United Family Food company – founded in 1981 and employing roughly 5, 000 people – and manufactures Milkita, a popular Indonesian brand of milk-based candies and snacks. The tragedy adds to a string of deadly industrial fires in Indonesia in recent years that have raised ongoing concerns over workplace safety and emergency preparedness.

The Associated Press and Reuters contributed to this report.

item.title: Social media users are eating huge amounts of carrots and shrimp for a natural tan
item.description: Dr. Navin Arora says the viral carrot tan from eating carrots, tomatoes and shrimp is real but no substitute for sunscreen and basic sun safety.
item.content:encoded:
Some social media users are "carrotmaxxing," "tomatomaxxing" and "shrimpmaxxing," in the hopes of getting a sun-kissed glow that lasts them all winter long.

The trend, which calls for eating large quantities of carrots, tomatoes and shrimp, or taking supplements packed with their compounds, relies on carotenoids, natural pigments found in certain foods, the New York Post recently reported.

The outlet highlighted wellness creators promoting raw carrots as a way to get a "carrot tan," including one who said she no longer gets fake tans, and followed two Atlanta moms who said they take a daily carotenoid supplement for a "healthy glow."

COULD 'HUMANMAXXING' ACTUALLY HELP YOU LIVE LONGER? HERE'S WHAT EXPERTS SAY

The supplement they take is a blend of three carotenoid pigments: beta-carotene, lycopene and astaxanthin, the compounds that give carrots, tomatoes, shrimp and salmon their color.

Wellness influencer Lee Tilghman Pollis, meanwhile, recently said on Instagram that raw carrots have given her "the best skin of my life and I will die on this hill."

Another influencer went viral on TikTok for her carrot tan, telling followers that she no longer gets fake tans or stays out in the sun and instead eats three to four large carrots a day for several months to build up her tan.

DOCTOR REVEALS 4 HIDDEN HEALTH RISKS OF SPENDING TOO MUCH TIME INDOORS

Experts say the skin-color change is real and generally harmless, but it's no substitute for basic sun-safety measures.

"Beta-carotene, lycopene and astaxanthin are fat-soluble pigments, and when you eat a lot of them they build up in the outermost layer of the skin," Dr. Navin Arora, a board-certified dermatologist and medical director of Borealis Dermatology in New York, told Fox News Digital.

NEW CALIFORNIA LAW WILL RESTRICT SALES OF SOME MUSCLE-BUILDING SUPPLEMENTS TO MINORS

The buildup can create a yellow or orange tint, often first visible on the palms, soles and around the nose.

There is no reliable dose for achieving a cosmetic change, Arora said. Small studies have found visible changes after about six weeks of eating extra servings of fruits and vegetables, though results can vary. The color also fades gradually after a person cuts back, he noted.

That pigment buildup, known as carotenemia, is generally harmless, Arora said, but skin that turns yellow-orange without a dietary change should be evaluated by a health care professional.

The food trick does avoid skin damage caused by UV exposure, which also raises the risk of skin cancer and premature aging.

"The carotenoid glow involves no UV damage at all, but it also gives you no meaningful sun protection," Arora warned. "'Carrot color' is not a substitute for sunscreen."

Arora cautioned against taking high-dose carotenoid supplements for appearance, though. High-dose beta-carotene supplements have been linked to increased lung cancer risk in people who smoke or used to smoke, according to the National Institutes of Health’s Office of Dietary Supplements.

TEST YOURSELF WITH OUR LATEST LIFESTYLE QUIZ

For people seeking a bronzed look, Arora recommends self-tanners, professional spray tans, bronzers or tinted sunscreen. He advises pairing them with broad-spectrum SPF 30 or higher every day.

"Eating a colorful, carotenoid-rich diet is great for your overall health," he said. "I’d treat the glow as a bonus, not the goal."

item.title: Iconic MTV star turns 60, shares her no-guilt approach to fitness, food and aging well
item.description: Daisy Fuentes shares her 20-minute strength training routine, menopause sleep tips and the guilt-free "anti-hustle era" that keeps her strong at 60.
item.content:encoded:
During her 1990s rise as an MTV icon and supermodel, Daisy Fuentes admitted that "being cute" was her top priority. 

Now, as she enters her 60s, the TV personality and lifestyle entrepreneur has traded superficial beauty pressures for a more grounded approach to health.

Speaking with Fox News Digital, Fuentes opened up about embracing a guilt-free "anti-hustle era" — sharing her 20-minute workouts, a "magical" sleep trick and the surprisingly simple habits that keep her rested and strong.

JENNIFER ANISTON’S SECRET TO STAYING FIT AT 57 STARTS WITH ONE SIMPLE WORKOUT ROUTINE

Fuentes’ health and wellness priorities have shifted a great deal in the decades since she started modeling and appearing on TV in her late teens and 20s, she shared.

"In that era, I was more focused on, how can I look better? How can I lose a few pounds to look better in certain clothes? It was very superficial. And as the years have passed, health and wellness has started to become an inside job," Fuentes said.

"When you start realizing that most of your life has already happened, how you want to live your life now … becomes more about being present and being able to enjoy the time that you have left," she added.

LONGEVITY DOCTOR REVEALS WHAT MATTERS MOST FOR AGING WELL, BEYOND PRICEY BIOHACKS

Amid the litany of longevity-focused tips and tricks circulating online, Fuentes said she strives to keep it simple and not be "obsessive" about health and wellness.

"On social media, depending on your algorithm, you can get bombarded and overwhelmed with all the [things] that you're supposed to be doing and not doing," she said.

"Yes, some of those things are smart … I do a lot of the things, but I also realized at a certain point that it's much more important to have fun, to be present, to not obsess, and to leave a little room for the unexpected."

As Fuentes entered her 50s, she started to experience some sleep challenges, which she attributed to fluctuating hormones during menopause.

"Balancing out my hormones [and] going on HRT [hormone replacement therapy] helped tremendously," she said. "It got me feeling back to my old self, where the minute I got in bed, I would do a little scrolling and all of a sudden my eyes would start closing."

10-MINUTE FITNESS HABIT CAN HELP ADULTS OVER 40 MAINTAIN MUSCLE AND STAY STRONG

Although Fuentes admits that she breaks a few traditional "sleep hygiene" rules — such as scrolling on her phone in bed – she does wear red-light-blocking glasses and strives to keep her social media algorithm strictly positive.

Fuentes said she relies on what she describes as a total "sensory experience" to stay asleep, including wearing a silk eye mask.

"Right as I'm going to sleep, I pop that mask on, and it's almost like magic," she said. "It does something to your brain. It relaxes you." She also uses an air purifier that provides white noise.

"Our room is set up for sleep," Fuentes said. "We don't hear anything, we don't see anything and it is a sensory experience … a routine that instantly prepares your mind for what it needs to do."

When it comes to fitness, Fuentes said she strives for consistency, but, above all, listens to her body.

A key component of her routine is strength training, which she does four or five times a week. "That doesn't mean it has to be long … I can do a full-body weight training in 20 minutes, and that's what's important to me right now," she said.

WOMEN WHO START COMMON HORMONE THERAPY IN THEIR 50S MAY HAVE 23% LOWER DEMENTIA RISK

Other mainstays of Fuentes’ fitness regimen include Pilates, walking and staying active outdoors. "That's what keeps me and my mind really feeling better," she said.

"Sometimes I get on a vibration plate with my weights and just do 15 minutes of that, doing a plank, doing some sit-ups on it, some squats — I just try to do whatever I can," Fuentes said.

"Some days I have more energy, some days I don't, and I don't beat myself up about it. I do what I feel like doing and as long as I'm doing something, I'm OK."

When it comes to nutrition, Fuentes’ biggest shifts over the last decade were driven by physical changes during menopause. Noticing stubborn weight gain around her midsection in her mid-50s, she said she scaled back to about two meals a day and eliminated mindless snacking.

CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR OUR HEALTH NEWSLETTER

"I try to make it very protein-based," she said. "I start my day with a coffee that already has 20 grams of protein in it ... And if I'm having a snack in the middle of the afternoon, it's going to be protein-packed yogurt with some nuts and berries."

CLICK HERE FOR MORE HEALTH STORIES

While Fuentes adopted a vegetarian, plant-based diet in her mid-40s, she emphasized that healthy eating doesn't require an "all-or-nothing" mindset, encouraging others to lean into more whole foods that match their lifestyle and preferences.

After decades of fast-paced working – both on and off-screen – Fuentes made a conscious decision in her late 40s to embrace a slower pace of life.

"Ambition that never ends is something that I think needs to be adjusted as we flow through life," she said, adding that she no longer desires to "be out there and be chosen" the way she did in her 30s.

"I started embracing the fact that I am in this era of my life where I don't want to work like when I was 30 … and it's OK to feel proud of myself for what I have accomplished," she said. "I don't want to feel guilty for enjoying the fruits of my labor, for enjoying my life now."

TEST YOURSELF WITH OUR LATEST LIFESTYLE QUIZ

When it comes to decompressing, Fuentes said she recharges by spending quiet time in the home spaces she loves decorating. Some of her favorite ways to unwind include reading, having tea with a friend, sitting in her backyard or taking an hour-long walk.

Fuentes shared her gratitude for being able to enjoy time with her husband, musician Richard Marx, whom she met in her mid-40s.

"Finding love and finding your person later in life made me feel so grateful to have the time to spend with him," she said. "Why would I want to pretend to be busy doing something when what really fills my heart is to be with him, to have fun, to do what I want to do right now?"

While Fuentes acknowledged that she is in a "privileged" and fortunate position, she pointed out that she spent decades sacrificing to earn it. 

Stepping into her "anti-hustle era" in her 50s and 60s, she said, is about questioning whether you are staying busy out of habit — or are ready to embrace a new, more fulfilling stage of life.
